about.title: The Americas II: Maya Writing, Calendars and the Andes
about.length_note: About 45 minutes, a little over the usual 40. This class has three big ideas (Maya writing and calendars, Maya kingdoms, and Andean knotted-cord records) and each needs room to be explained one step at a time. I could not find a reliable source for what was happening in Europe, Africa or Asia during the Classic Maya centuries, so the 'outside the Americas' part is short and uses only what I read. Class 13 puts everything on one timeline.

say.text: Welcome to class 12. Last time we met Caral, the Olmec and early cities. Today: how the Maya wrote and counted time, how Maya kings ruled, and how Andean people kept records with knots.

show.text: The Americas II: Maya Writing, Calendars and the Andes

say.text: First, where are we? Maya cities stood across what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras. Tikal is in Guatemala. Copán is in Honduras. We will come back to both.

show.text: Map of southern Mexico and Central America. Marked: Chichén Itzá (Mexico), Tikal (Guatemala), Copán (Honduras).

say.text: Before the Maya script we can read, there are older signs. One is the Cascajal block: a slab of stone with 62 characters unlike any seen before in Mesoamerica.

show.text: A greenish stone slab, about the size of a writing tablet, covered in 62 small carved signs.

say.text: Here is a site-style puzzle: made once, found later. Carved roughly 950 to 600 BCE. Dug up by road builders in the late 1990s. Reported to the world in September 2006.

show.text: c. 950-600 BCE: carved | late 1990s: found by road builders | Sept 2006: reported in Science

ask.q: Who first dug up the Cascajal block?
ask.why: Road builders found it in a pile of debris in the late 1990s. Scholars announced it in 2006.

say.text: A careful note. The case for this script rests on one block. Some scholars say it is true writing. Others call it a kind of early sign system.

show.text: One block

say.text: Two later scripts. Zapotec writing: the earliest known stone is dated about 500 to 600 BCE. Epi-Olmec, or Isthmian, script ran from about 300 BCE to 250 CE.

show.text: Zapotec: Danzante stone, c. 500-600 BCE | Epi-Olmec: c. 300 BCE-250 CE, La Mojarra Stela 1

say.text: Now the Maya script. It mixes two kinds of sign. Some signs are word signs, called logograms. Others stand for single sounds, called syllable signs. Experts call this logosyllabic.

show.text: Logosyllabic = word signs + syllable signs

say.text: An example. A word sign can mean 'jaguar' or 'shield'. A syllable sign is a sound like 'pa' or 'ma'. A scribe could use either, or blend them.

show.text: Word signs (logograms): jaguar, shield | Syllable signs: pa, ma

ask.q: How did the Maya script work?
ask.right: It mixed word signs and syllable signs
wrong: It was an alphabet of letters
It used only pictures, with no sounds
ask.why: It was logosyllabic: some signs stood for words and others for syllables. There was no Maya alphabet.

say.text: For centuries nobody could read it. In the 1500s, Bishop Diego de Landa tried to match Maya signs to Spanish letters. He did not realise the script was not alphabetic.

show.text: A page of de Landa's 'alphabet': Spanish letters beside Maya signs.

say.text: The turning point came in the 1950s. Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov saw that de Landa's signs were not letters but syllables. He tested this on a sign pair beside a picture of a turkey, which is cutz in Maya.

show.text: cu + tzu = cutz (turkey)

ask.q: What did Knorozov realise about de Landa's signs?
ask.right: They stood for syllables, not letters
wrong: They were drawings of gods only
They were copied from Egyptian hieroglyphs
ask.why: Knorozov treated de Landa's signs as a syllabary. That opened the way to reading the script.

say.text: Then Tatiana Proskouriakoff showed that the dates and texts on monuments told of real rulers and the main events of their lives. Many other scholars added to the work after that.

show.text: Monuments record real kings

ask.q: What did Proskouriakoff show about Maya inscriptions?
ask.right: They record real rulers and the events of their lives
wrong: They are only maps of the stars
They are copies of de Landa's alphabet
ask.why: She showed the dates in the texts referred to rulers and major events, so the monuments carry history.

say.text: The Maya also wrote books called codices. When Knorozov was starting out, only three were known: the Dresden, Madrid and Paris codices. Few Maya books survive.

show.text: Dresden codex | Madrid codex | Paris codex

say.text: Now time. The Maya kept several calendars at once. The first is the Tzolk'in, a 260-day count. It pairs 20 day names with the numbers 1 to 13.

show.text: 260 days = 20 names x 13 numbers

ask.q: How many different days are in the Tzolk'in, if 20 day names pair with 13 numbers?
ask.why: 20 times 13 is 260. Each name-and-number pair is used once before the count starts again.

say.text: The Tzolk'in was used to arrange tasks and ceremonies, and for fortune-telling. The 'years' of the Tzolk'in were not counted. It is the sacred count.

show.text: Tzolk'in: the sacred count

say.text: The second calendar is the Haab, the 365-day solar year. It has 18 months of 20 days. Then comes a short extra period of five days at the end.

show.text: The five extra days at the end of the Haab

ask.q: 18 months of 20 days, plus 5 extra days: how many days in the Haab?
ask.why: 18 times 20 is 360. Adding the 5 extra days makes 365.

say.text: Run the two counts together, like two gears. The same pair of dates only comes back after 18,980 days. That is about 52 years, and it is called the Calendar Round.

show.text: Maya counts, in days

ask.q: About how long is one Calendar Round?
ask.why: It takes 18,980 days, which is 52 Haab years, for the same Tzolk'in and Haab pair to meet again.

say.text: A 52-year loop is too short for a long history. So the Maya also used the Long Count. It counts days from a starting point in the mythic past, which scholars place in 3114 BCE.

show.text: Long Count: days counted from 3114 BCE

ask.q: What does the Long Count do?
ask.right: It counts days from a fixed starting point
wrong: It names the twenty days of the Tzolk'in
It counts only the five extra days
ask.why: The Long Count is a running tally of days since a mythic start. It does not repeat like the Calendar Round.

say.text: These calendars are not only history. Many groups in the Guatemalan highlands still use the Calendar Round. Some Maya communities still use the 260-day count today.

show.text: Still in use today

say.text: Maya astronomers watched Venus. The Dresden Codex holds a Venus table. And some Maya wars, called star wars, were linked to Venus events.

show.text: A page of the Dresden Codex with columns of day signs and numbers for the Venus table.

say.text: Now who ruled? Not one Maya empire. Each city-state had its own dynasty of kings. In the Classic period there were dozens, including Tikal, Palenque, Copán and Calakmul.

show.text: Tikal | Palenque | Copán | Calakmul

say.text: The king was called a k'uhul ajaw, or 'holy lord'. One person held religious, military and political power together. Power was not split among separate offices.

show.text: k'uhul ajaw = holy lord

ask.right: A Maya city-state's holy lord, who held religious, military and political power
ask.why: The title means 'holy lord'. Classic Maya states focused religious, military and political power on this ruler.

say.text: Kings recorded their rule in stone. They raised carved monuments called stelae. Maya law is harder: I did not find a reliable source on written law codes, so I will not guess.

show.text: A tall carved stela standing in a plaza, a king in headdress above columns of glyphs.

say.text: Site spotlight: Tikal. Its royal line is the oldest yet known in the Maya Lowlands. It began around the turn of the 1st century AD. At least 33 rulers are known, from the 1st to the 9th century.

show.text: 33+ known rulers of Tikal

say.text: The big rivals were Tikal and Calakmul. In the 650s Calakmul drove Tikal's ruler out of his city. Tikal came back. In 695 its king Jasaw Chan K'awiil defeated Calakmul and captured its king.

show.text: 657: Calakmul attacks Tikal | 695: Tikal defeats Calakmul

ask.q: Who won the key battle in 695?
ask.why: Tikal defeated Calakmul in 695 and captured its king.

say.text: Small cities picked sides. In 734 the king of Quiriguá took the title k'uhul ajaw. That declared Quiriguá independent of Copán.

show.text: 734: Quiriguá breaks from Copán

ask.q: What did the king of Quiriguá do in 734?
ask.right: He took the title k'uhul ajaw and declared independence from Copán
ask.why: Taking the 'holy lord' title showed Quiriguá no longer served Copán.

say.text: Site spotlight: Copán, built then found. It thrived in the Classic period. Spanish explorers saw its ruins in the late 1500s. Stephens and Catherwood 'rediscovered' it in 1839.

show.text: Classic period: city thrives | late 1500s: Spanish explorers | 1839: Stephens and Catherwood

ask.q: In which year did Stephens and Catherwood reach Copán?
ask.why: They arrived in 1839. Their drawings later showed the Maya built these cities.

say.text: Catherwood's drawings were very exact. The pair described 44 sites, many for the first time. They helped show the Maya built these cities themselves.

show.text: 44 sites described

say.text: Religion next. The Popol Vuh is a K'iche' Maya book. It holds the oldest Maya myth kept whole. It began as spoken tradition and was copied by a friar in the early 1700s.

show.text: A page of a handwritten colonial manuscript, the Popol Vuh.

say.text: The ballgame was part of that story. In the Popol Vuh, the Hero Twins play against the lords of the underworld. Ball courts stood at the heart of Maya cities, signs of wealth and power.

show.text: The Hero Twins' ballgame

say.text: Did the Maya sacrifice ballplayers? Human sacrifice did happen, often tied to war. But scholars say it was not an integral part of the game. The idea grew partly from the Popol Vuh and skull carvings.

show.text: Sacrifice: real, but not part of every game

ask.q: What do scholars say about sacrifice and the ballgame?
ask.right: Sacrifice happened but was not an integral part of the game
wrong: Sacrifice never happened among the Maya
The game was only a children's game
ask.why: Sacrifice did occur, often in war. Experts say it was not an integral part of the game.

say.text: A real case. In 562, Tikal's ruler Wak Chan K'awiil was captured and sacrificed by soldiers from Caracol. His death ended his line at Tikal. Defeat in war could be fatal.

show.text: 562: Tikal's ruler captured

say.text: Now we cross to South America. Different place, different way of keeping records. Let us start with a very old temple site high in the Andes: Chavín de Huántar.

show.text: The Andes: Chavín, textiles and khipu

say.text: Chavín de Huántar lies in the Peruvian highlands, about 3,200 metres up. It was a major religious and pilgrimage centre. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1985.

show.text: 3,200 metres above sea level

say.text: When was it built? From about 900 to 200 BCE it was an important religious and economic centre. Some sources start the building earlier, so dates differ a little.

show.text: c. 900 BCE-200 BCE: important religious and economic centre

say.text: Inside are dark stone passages. The temple holds the Lanzón, a carved stone figure of the main deity: a human body with a feline head. Dark halls and echoing sound may have made visits feel powerful.

show.text: A narrow stone passage inside the temple, dark, leading to a tall carved stone shaft.

say.text: Now 'found again'. In 1873 naturalist Antonio Raimondi visited and called the structure a fortress. In 1919 Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello began investigating it. He argued it was a 'mother culture' of Andean civilization.

show.text: c. 900-200 BCE: used | 1873: Raimondi visits | 1919: Tello begins digging

ask.q: Who began investigating Chavín de Huántar in 1919?
ask.why: Raimondi visited in 1873. Tello began his investigations in 1919.

say.text: Chavín carvings show powerful animals: jaguars, snakes, crocodiles and eagles. This art style spread widely across the Andes. And cloth carried the style: Chavín-era textiles look much alike from region to region.

show.text: Jaguars | Snakes | Crocodiles | Eagles

say.text: Why do we know so much about Andean cloth? Dry air helped preserve it. Tello and his team collected 394 textiles from the Paracas burials, a separate culture on the Peruvian coast.

show.text: 394 Paracas textiles

say.text: Textiles also lead us to khipu, the Andean answer to writing. Khipu are knotted cords, a textile record-keeping device. The Inka used them. Their empire ran from about 1400 to 1532, well over a thousand years after Chavín.

show.text: Khipu = knot

say.text: How is a khipu built? A main cord has many pendant cords hanging from it. The cords carry knots. Colour, fibre and twist direction all vary. A typical khipu averages about 60 pendant cords.

show.text: A khipu: one thick cord across the top with many thinner coloured cords hanging down, each tied with knots.

say.text: Specially trained record keepers, called khipukamayuq, tied and read the cords. A chronicler says every community had at least four khipu accountants, all keeping the same records. That gave a check on mistakes.

show.text: Khipukamayuq = knot-maker

ask.q: Why did each community have four khipu accountants?
ask.right: They kept the same records, so the accounts could be checked
wrong: Each one wrote a different language
They were the only people allowed to farm
They traded the cords for cacao
ask.why: The chronicler says all four kept the same records, a system of checks and balances.

say.text: What did khipu record? Mostly numbers and administration, like a census. A Harvard student, with Gary Urton, matched six khipu to a Spanish census of 132 people. The cord ties seemed to match people's social status.

show.text: 6 khipu matched a census of 132 people

ask.q: What are khipu best known for recording?
ask.right: Counts and administrative records, such as a census
ask.why: Khipu are known to have kept census and other administrative data.

say.text: Back to daily life among the Maya. Most people were farmers. They grew maize, beans, squash and chili peppers. They used slash-and-burn, terraces and raised fields. Maize became tortillas, tamales and a drink called atole.

show.text: Maize | Beans | Squash | Chili peppers

ask.q: Which crop was the foundation of the Maya diet?
ask.why: Maize was the foundation, eaten as tortillas, tamales and atole.

say.text: The Maya traded widely. Goods included obsidian, jade, salt, feathers, textiles and cacao. Classic cities had markets. They made tools from obsidian, jade and other stone, and used no metal until much later.

show.text: Obsidian | Jade | Salt | Quetzal feathers | Cacao

say.text: Andean trade was busy too. In the Chavín period, long-distance trade rose sharply. People exchanged pottery, shell, stone, wool, textiles, metals and dried fish.

show.text: Pottery | Shell | Wool and textiles | Metals | Dried fish

say.text: Outside the Americas: I could not source the Classic-era world scene, so here is what I read. In 1839, the year Copán was rediscovered, Austen Layard set out on the long journey that led him to dig at Nimrud in 1845 and at Nineveh, a Mesopotamian city from class 3, in 1847. Class 13 builds the full timeline.

show.text: 1839: Copán explored | 1839: Layard begins digging at Nineveh

say.text: Let us pull it together. Maya scribes wrote with word and syllable signs. They counted time with three linked calendars. Kings ruled city-states that fought and allied. The Andes used knots, not writing.

show.text: Maya script | Calendars | City-states | Khipu

ask.right: Maya: logosyllabic script. Andes: khipu knotted cords
wrong: Maya: an alphabet. Andes: the Long Count
Maya: one empire. Andes: no records at all
ask.why: The Maya used a script of word and syllable signs. Andean people, in the Inka period, used khipu cords.

frame_of_reference.when: c. 900 BCE (Cascajal block); Chavín de Huántar in use from c. 900 BCE
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: No non-American events for this date were found in the sources read. Class 13 places the Americas beside Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus and China.
Austen Layard began digging at Nineveh, in Mesopotamia, the year Stephens and Catherwood explored Copán.
The Spanish began conquering Mesoamerica and soon stamped out the ballgame, linked to sacrifice and 'idolatrous' practices.
The Spanish conquest of Peru ended the Inka empire, which had lasted from about 1400.
Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov, working from Moscow, proposed the key that opened the Maya script.

other_side.claim: The Cascajal block is the earliest writing in the Americas.
other_side.other_view: Scholars disagree on whether it is true writing. The case rests on a single block with no known relatives. The Zapotec script, from about 500 BCE, was long thought the earliest. The partial reading of Epi-Olmec script is also disputed.
Sacrifice did happen, often in the context of war. But scholars note it was not an integral part of the game. The modern idea owes much to the Popol Vuh and to skull art on ball courts.

other_side.claim: Chavín de Huántar was the 'mother culture' of Andean civilization.
other_side.other_view: Tello argued this for decades. Later work, especially radiocarbon dating, has narrowed his claims and refined how Chavín relates to other sites. Sources also give somewhat different building dates for the temple.

other_side.claim: Khipu were a kind of writing.
other_side.other_view: Khipu are well understood as number records. Some researchers think they may also hold narrative information, but this is unproven. About a third of khipu do not follow the usual decimal pattern, so much remains unread.
